newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Markets absorb US rate rise, euro uncertainty -BIS.
newsitem.headline: Markets absorb US rate rise, euro uncertainty -BIS.

text.p: Financial markets were quick to absorb new questions over Europe's single currency and the hike in U.S. interest rates in the first quarter of 1997 with activity in the international syndicated loan and securities markets remaining brisk, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said on Sunday.

However, BIS questioned whether banks were sufficiently prudent right now in light of risks stemming from large cross-border investment flows, the unusally long U.S. expansion, new credit risk management techniques, practical implementation of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and lack of internal risk controls.

Although the Federal Reserve's increase in U.S. interest rate rise in March was widely anticipated, the move challenged the prevailing mood of optimism and BIS noted there were doubts as to whether the recent market correction had run its course.

"When viewed in relation to greater official reliance on market forces than on rigid supervisory prescriptions, these developments should put a premium on more prudent behaviour by market participants," BIS said in its latest quarterly report on International Banking and Financial Markets.
But the disruption to markets from the U.S. rate hike proved short-lived and less abrubt than in early 1994, when the Federal Reserve startled markets by raising rates.
"On balance the search for yields and the related process of international portfolio diversification were not fundamentally called into question," BIS said.
While ample liquidity supported financial activity, BIS also said deeper underlying changes in the world financial system might explain why markets absorbed the shock.

These changes include the more systematic use of collateral in various type of lending, consolidation already achieved in the financial industry, improved economic and financial fundamentals in most regions and widespread anticipation of the Federal Reserve's tighter monetary policy stance.

In the syndicated loan market new announcements rose to $114.4 billion, significantly above the first 1996 quarter, with a further rise in deals related to mergers and acquisitions, but also a growing proportion of project-related lending.

In the securities markets a total of $206.4 billion in new bonds were announced, just off the all-time high in early 1996. After excluding repayments, net issuance was $137.6 billion, comparable to the average in 1996.
With plenty of loanable funds, BIS said spread differentials between prime and non-prime borrowers in the syndicated loan market eroded further, encouraging the entry of new borrowers.

There was also a tendency for new hybrid structures where arrangements cross over between bank loans and securities. This is partially due to the growing involvement of institutional investors and investment banks in bank lending.

Detailed statistics for the fourth quarter of 1996 gave further evidence of a growing dichotomy between stagnating interbank business and buoyant transactions with non-bank customers, whether financial or non-financial.

The retreat of Japanese banks from international lending also continued in 1996 with Japanese' banks' share of international banking assets dropping three percentage points to 22 percent, a 13-year low.
Despite this drop, Japanese banks still rank first, ahead of German banks with a share of 17 percent and U.S. and French banks, each with a share of 11 percent.
BIS noted that Swiss banks moved up in the ranks and are now ranked fifth, ahead of Italian and UK banks.
The growth of lending to emerging countries from banks in the Group of 10 (G10) leading nations also accelerated in the fourth quarter, reaching a new record of $40.4 billion.
Not only was there an increase to Asian and Latin American borrowers, but also to Eastern Europe, BIS said.

However, reflecting continued instability and uncertainty in Russia, BIS noted that interbank credit flows to Russia appear to be rechanneled abroad in the form of deposits in foreign financial centres.
Capital inflow to Russia jumped by $3.1 billion in the fourth quarter of 1996, but during the same period Russian banks deposited $2.4 billion abroad.

In the derivatives market, aggregate turnover of exchange-traded contracts rose seven percent to about 300 million in the 1997 first quarter, the first rise after three consecutive quarters of contraction.
In the swap and Over-The-Counter (OTC) interest market in 1996 activity also remained brisk with the total stock of outstanding contracts rising 37 percent from end-1995 to $24.3 trillion.
With the bulk of derivatives business taking place on the OTC market, BIS questioned whether derivatives exchanges would face further decline.

"While the two markets remain complementary, the relative importance of exchanges could decline further owing to advances in risk mangement techniques and to some inherent advantages of OTC instruments," BIS said.
